questions.question: In 1783, which two French brothers launched the first practical hot-air balloon?
questions.note: Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier flew their first public balloon at Annonay in June 1783.

questions.question: Deposed after France's defeat in the Franco-Prussian War, the last French emperor, Napoleon III, died in exile in 1873 in which Kent town?
questions.note: Napoleon III lived and died at Camden Place in Chislehurst before his remains were later moved to Farnborough.

questions.question: The savoury, umami flavour of Lea & Perrins Worcestershire sauce comes largely from which small fermented fish?
questions.note: Invented in Worcester in the 1830s, the sauce ferments anchovies for months to build its taste.

questions.question: How many overseas régions (the DROM) does France have?
questions.note: France's five overseas régions are Guadeloupe, Martinique, French Guiana, Réunion and Mayotte.

questions.question: Which English author created the character Peter Rabbit?
questions.note: The Tale of Peter Rabbit was published by Frederick Warne & Co. in 1902.

questions.question: In French, the everyday word 'un slip' refers to which item of clothing?
questions.note: A classic false friend: French 'un slip' means underpants or briefs.

questions.question: The world's first ATM (cash machine) opened in 1967 at a Barclays branch in which north London suburb?
questions.note: The machine, devised by John Shepherd-Barron, was unveiled at Barclays Enfield on 27 June 1967.

questions.question: After Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685, French Protestant Huguenots fled to England; which East London district did they make the heart of the silk-weaving trade?
questions.note: Huguenot refugees brought advanced silk-weaving skills to Spitalfields, turning it into the centre of Britain's luxury silk trade.

questions.question: Beef bourguignon, a classic French stew of beef braised in red wine, traditionally comes from which region of France?
questions.note: The dish and its wine both take their name from the Burgundy (Bourgogne) region.

questions.question: The Giant's Causeway, shown here with its famous basalt columns, lies in which part of the United Kingdom?
questions.imageAlt: Interlocking hexagonal basalt columns forming a rocky coastal pavement by the sea
questions.imageCredit: Giant's Causeway · Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA (credit at source)
questions.note: On the County Antrim coast, its 40,000 columns became Northern Ireland's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.

questions.question: Which French composer wrote the opera Carmen?
questions.note: Bizet's Carmen premiered at the Opéra-Comique in Paris in March 1875 — he died just months later, before its huge success.

questions.question: In English, the word 'gaffe' (borrowed from French) means what?
questions.answer: An embarrassing blunder or social mistake
questions.note: English took 'gaffe' from French to mean a foolish, embarrassing error made in public.

questions.question: Which British scientist invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN?
questions.note: He wrote his proposal for the Web at CERN in 1989 and built the first browser and server soon after.

questions.question: Green Chartreuse, the French herbal liqueur, is famously distilled by monks of which Catholic religious order?
questions.note: Carthusian monks have made the secret 130-plant liqueur since the 18th century.

questions.question: What was the code name of the 1940 operation that evacuated over 338,000 British and French troops from the beaches of Dunkirk?
questions.note: Operation Dynamo ran from 26 May to 4 June 1940, aided by a flotilla of civilian 'little ships'.

questions.question: The 2001 film Amélie is set in which hilltop district of Paris?
questions.note: Jean-Pierre Jeunet's film, starring Audrey Tautou, is a love letter to the Montmartre neighbourhood.

questions.question: What is the largest island of Scotland's Inner Hebrides?
questions.note: Skye is the largest and best known of the Inner Hebrides, linked to the mainland by the Skye Bridge.

questions.question: In French, 'un flipper' is which piece of amusement-arcade equipment?
questions.note: A pseudo-anglicism: in France 'un flipper' is a pinball machine, named after its flippers.

questions.question: What is the name of the great survey of English landholdings commissioned by William the Conqueror and completed in 1086?
questions.note: The Norman survey recorded the value and resources of estates across England and is now held at the National Archives.

questions.question: Concorde, the Franco-British supersonic airliner shown here, made its first prototype flight in 1969 from which French city?
questions.imageAlt: A slender white supersonic airliner with a long drooping needle nose
questions.imageCredit: British Airways Concorde G-BOAC · Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA (credit at source)
questions.note: Concorde 001 first flew from Toulouse on 2 March 1969, a joint project of France's Aérospatiale and Britain's BAC.

questions.question: Traditional Melton Mowbray pork pies are baked free-standing, without a tin, using which type of pastry?
questions.note: The lard-and-boiling-water dough sets firm enough to hold the pie's bow-shaped sides without a tin.

questions.question: What is the highest summit of the French Pyrenees — the highest Pyrenean peak lying partly on French soil?
questions.note: At 3,298 m the Vignemale is the highest French Pyrenean summit, though the range's overall highest peak, Aneto, lies entirely in Spain.

questions.question: Which sculptor created the Angel of the North, the giant steel figure near Gateshead shown here?
questions.imageAlt: A giant rust-coloured steel human figure with huge straight aeroplane-like wings
questions.imageCredit: Angel of the North · Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA (credit at source)
questions.note: Gormley's 20-metre steel sculpture, with a 54-metre wingspan, was installed beside the A1 in 1998.

questions.question: In the south-west of France (around Toulouse and Bordeaux), what word do locals use instead of 'pain au chocolat'?
questions.note: The south-west says 'chocolatine' — a regional split so fierce it has even been raised in the French parliament.

questions.question: The SEPECAT Jaguar strike aircraft, first flown in 1968, was jointly developed by France and which other country?
questions.note: SEPECAT was a joint venture between France's Breguet and Britain's BAC — one of several Franco-British aviation projects of the era.

questions.question: In the 1605 Gunpowder Plot, Guy Fawkes and his fellow conspirators planned to blow up the House of Lords and kill which king of England?
questions.note: The failed Catholic plot against the Protestant king is still marked each 5 November as Bonfire Night.

questions.question: English keeps Anglo-Saxon names for the live animals (cow, pig, sheep) but uses words from which language for their meat (beef, pork, mutton)?
questions.note: The split dates from 1066: Norman-French rulers named the meat at the table while English farmers kept the animals' names.

questions.question: France's national motto 'Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité' translates into English as which three words?
questions.note: The motto dates from the French Revolution and is carved on public buildings across France.

questions.question: After leaving England, the Greenwich (Prime) Meridian next reaches the continental European coast at Villers-sur-Mer, in which French région?
questions.note: Villers-sur-Mer in Calvados is the only French seaside resort sitting on the Greenwich Meridian.

questions.question: Baroness Orczy's novel The Scarlet Pimpernel, in which an Englishman rescues aristocrats from the guillotine, is set during the revolution in which country?
questions.note: The 1905 British novel, set during the Reign of Terror, more or less invented the 'secret-identity hero' template.
